prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, and models of dynamic industries, which transformed empirical industrial organisation and the measurement of market power and welfare

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B013. I now prefer B001, and the reason is the exchange on attribution and maturity, not the number of members who rank it first. My own standard is new evidence combined with an explanatory framework, applied to every field. B013 meets it well, but its credit boundary was my main concern and the exchange has not resolved it. Enflo and I both reject the two-name versions, so the choice between Katz and Dorn for the third slot remains, and the Committee would also have to choose between the task framework and the trade-shock strand as the core. The magnitudes and persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated, and the task framework shares ground with the 2024 recognition. B001 does not have these problems. The demand-estimation core is a jointly authored result with a named trio. Its maturity is not disputed by anyone, and the sensitivities of the method (numerical implementation, instruments, functional form) are documented and have been worked on. I accept the toolkit-versus-discovery concern. I would answer it as follows. The method changed what economists can credibly say about substitution, markups and welfare, and it produces counterfactuals that earlier reduced-form work could not. It has also spread beyond industrial organisation. That is a measurement advance that changed practice, which I think meets the common criterion. As a labour economist who works mostly with quasi-experimental designs, I value credibility of identification more than most colleagues do. I therefore take the identification caveats on structural work seriously, but I see them as qualifications and not as grounds for disqualification. I propose Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn with a method-level citation that keeps the dynamic-industry framework as part of the achievement. I would not widen it to every production-function or programme-level strand. I would keep a single achievement. A second part would not fit inside three names without weakening both citations, and B013 and B001 share no names.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is that this honours a toolkit, and a Committee that weighs methods below substantive findings could reasonably go another way. The seven credited names on the ballot entry cover several strands, so the three-name cut is a judgement. Bresnahan is the most serious omission, and Reiss, Benkard and Levin also have claims. I am moving away from B013 because of unresolved attribution and settledness. Its science is strong, and its scientific merit and policy influence are at least as large as B001's. The consequence is that B013 may be deferred even though the work is important. A prize awarded now would be cleanest for B001, but the Committee may judge that B013's societal relevance outweighs its attribution cost. I cannot show that either weighting is wrong.

responses.point: Krusell proposes Pakes, Berry and Bresnahan for B001. He argues that Bresnahan's new empirical IO programme and his early market-power estimation are foundational, and that the Levinsohn version is not a scientific error.
responses.response: I take the Bresnahan case seriously, and my view remains that the choice between the two names is a judgement call and not a scientific error. I keep Levinsohn because a method-level citation should name the authors of the jointly written result that defines the estimator. Dropping a co-author of the central paper creates a sharper attribution problem than leaving out an adjacent pioneer. I read Bresnahan's claim as a stronger fit for a programme-level citation on the new empirical IO. That is a different and more diffuse achievement, and a three-name cap does not accommodate it well. If the Committee chose that framing I would accept Bresnahan in that slot, but I would want the citation to be reworded so that it does not credit the BLP paper itself.

responses.point: Hassler proposes Autor and Hanson only for B013, and he argues that the unit of the B001 prize should be defined narrowly, as demand and competition estimation plus the dynamic-industry framework.
responses.response: On B001 I agree with the narrow unit. Adding production-function estimation or the wider empirical-IO agenda would blur what is being recognised and reopen the attribution problem. On B013 I still disagree with the two-name version, because dropping Katz removes the longest-confirmed part of the programme. The Acemoglu point does persuade me that any B013 citation would have to rest on the wage-structure and trade-exposure evidence and not on the task framework in general. That narrowing is part of why I now judge B013 less ready than B001. The remaining question is not whether the science is good but whether it can be defined as a single achievement with a defensible trio.

responses.point: Enflo also prefers B013 and argues that Autor links the two strands and that a citation covering both is the most honest framing. She rejects the view that a toolkit should automatically outrank an empirical-conceptual contribution.
responses.response: I agree with her on the second point. A toolkit should not outrank an empirical-conceptual contribution by default, and I do not think B001 wins simply because it is a toolkit. My answer to the chair's question is that B013 can be defined as a single strand only at a cost. A trade-shock-only strand points to Autor, Dorn and Hanson and drops Katz. A skill-and-task strand points to Autor and Katz and drops the evidence that changed policy debate. Her both-strands framing is the most honest description of the work, but it is also the one that forces the Katz-versus-Dorn choice. I have no principled rule for settling that choice, and that is what moves me. I still list B013 as my first alternative and would not regard it as a poor outcome.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first. He answers the toolkit concern by saying the discovery is a measurement capability that changed what can be known about competition and welfare, and he ranks B013 lower because the China-shock results are debated and attribution is split.
responses.response: His test is the one I would use: whether practice changed and whether the results held up. B001 meets both on the evidence the members cite. I accept the maturity point about B013 in part. The debate has refined the central patterns and not overturned them, so I would not call B013 immature, but the debate over magnitude and persistence adds to the attribution problem. Where I differ is on how much confidence the evidence supports. The sensitivities to numerical choices and instruments are real, and I would want the citation to say that the method enables measurement under stated assumptions, not that it settles market-power questions. I would also accept, as he says, that a stronger B013 case may exist in a later year.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B013 as his clear second choice and says he would be comfortable with it as the alternative if B001 stalls. He also asks whether a second achievement could be added within the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree that B013 is the natural alternative, and I treat it that way. On a second achievement, I would not add one. B001 already uses all three names, and there is no overlap with B013 that would let two parts share credit. Adding a part would leave at most one name per part or force a trade-off that weakens both citations. A single-achievement prize is cleaner and avoids the attribution problems of B013. If B001 stalls, the Committee should then decide B013 as its own question, with an explicit rule for Katz versus Dorn, and not combine it with B001.

uncertainties: Whether Levinsohn or Bresnahan belongs in the third slot, and whether the Committee prefers a method-level citation or a programme-level one on the new empirical IO.

Whether the Committee gives a measurement toolkit the same weight as a substantive empirical discovery. My own view has moved toward treating B001 as a measurement discovery, but it could be read as a toolkit.

Which of the documented sensitivities (numerical implementation, instrument choice, functional form) would change a merger-review or welfare conclusion in practice. Evidence on that from replication or regulatory case studies would sharpen my view, and I rely on background knowledge only.
Whether B013 can be defined as a single achievement with a defensible trio (Katz or Dorn), and how far the China-shock magnitudes and the 2024 recognition limit it.
I have not independently verified any citation, adoption or regulatory-use claims.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1: none apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on B001, B013 or B002. I use administrative data and quasi-experimental designs, which is methodologically adjacent to B013 and B017, but I have no tie to any credited name on those entries. Moving from B013 to B001 reflects the attribution and maturity reasoning above and not any connection to the B001 names. I have no apparent connection to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn or Bresnahan. These ties are disclosed, not adjudicated.
